messages.subject_clean: distance in R via mrds, Distance
messages.body_plain:
Dear List, Jeff and Dave,

I would like to move my distance sampling analysis workflow to R (with
which I have greater familiarity than DISTANCE). I have encountered a
number of difficulties in making this transition. I've been working through
a couple of different example projects that I have completed in DISTANCE in
R in order to validate the R output. These data are from single-observer
point count data, and distances are truncated and binned. I have called the
ds() function in package Distance and ddf() function in mrds. The results
have been highly inconsistent and produced numerous types of errors.

As a first pass, I used the ds() function to facilitate detection and
density estimation in one step. For one dataset (Song Sparrows), ds()
faithfully reproduces the output from DISTANCE with a cds model of global
detection probability with a hazard rate key function. ds(), however, does
not reproduce the DISTANCE results, using other key functions, instead
returning the following error:

Error in model$meta.data : $ operator is invalid for atomic vectors

In an effort to work around this error, I began working directly with
ddf(), since it seemed like something was problematic in the way that ds()
was wrapping up my data and passing it to ddf(). While ddf() returned a
model fit, it did not match the output from DISTANCE. Recognizing that it
may have been the way my dataset were structured, I have used both a
dataset that I have constructed to meet ddf() expectations, as well as
using the dataset returned by the output of the successful hazard-rate
model returned in the ddf object from ds(). This does not resolve the issue.

With a second dataset (Yellow Warblers), ds() reproduced DISTANCE output
with the key function (half-normal) with no adjustment parameters, but did
not accurately fit the  models with adjustment parameters, which also
happened to be better fitting models in DISTANCE. I also encountered many
of the same issues as with the previous dataset, including the
model$meta.data error and the following FORTRAN error when fitting a hazard
rate key function with hermite polynomial adjustment function:

Error in if (any(interp)) y[interp] <- .Fortran(C_bvalus, n =
as.integer(n),  :
  missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed

I am hesitant to move forward to more complex mcds analyses until I can
resolve my issues with more basic cds models, although one or two brief
attempts to add mcds covariates failed.

This is my second attempt at calling DISTANCE directly from R, and as I
recall the first attempt failed due to similar issues, where not all of the
key functions produced reliable output that matched that from DISTANCE. I
would appreciate any advice, thoughts or resources that more experienced
members of the list (or the package developers) have to share! I have
searched high and low for possible solutions but have not found anything
that seems to address the particular issues that I am encountering.

Thanks!
--
Joshua Goldberg
Research Associate
Natural Sciences 305
The University of Montana
Missoula, MT 59812

There may be a software problem, but the quantity of data you have will
not make for a defensible analysis.  You have no replication of
transects within your strata (so there can be no measure of variability
in encounter rate-a fundamental component of a density estimate).
Similarly you have far too few sightings to do a reasonable job of
fitting a detection function.

Have a look through section 7.2 on survey design in Buckland et al.
(2001) and if you still think your data need to be analysed, you can
send you Distance project to me directly (rather than via the list).

messages.body_plain:
You cannot use AIC as a comparison across different truncation distances.
 It will likely continue to decrease as the truncation increases and as you
noted the CV will increase.  You should select a truncation distance and
then use AIC to compare models. You should look at the fit (particularly
near x=0) to evaluate the best truncation distance.  You really only want
to truncate if the tail of the distribution is causing a poor fit at the
origin (x=0) and that can cause differences in the density estimates.
 --jeff

messages.body_plain:
Sandro:

Here are some quick thoughts about what you present:

Of the cosine vs. polynomial adjustment term contrast you present, there
seems to be evidence to prefer the cosine adjustment terms. You then
show that with truncation and the cosine adjustments you get "better
fit" (you do not quantify what you mean by better fit; did the
untruncated models fit?), but at the loss of some precision.  It is not
surprising that you lose some precision as measured by CV (but remember
CV is ratio of SE(DS)/DS); given that your point estimate (DS) decreased
a small bit (7.2 vs 6.7) that may be the explanation for the small rise
in CV.

Two things to keep in mind:
a) it is not necessary to have best fit, only necessary to have models
with adequate fit.  Parsimony argues that you should use a model that
only fits your data (and no more); so if your goodness of fit statistic
is acceptable, then stop.

b) you might consider asking Distance not to report the estimates of
density while you are performing your model selection, that way your
decisions about models are not coloured by the estimates models produce.

Finally as Jeff just noted, changing truncation changes data, and AIC
cannot be used for model selection to determine truncation.

messages.body_plain:
It occurred to me that some folks may not quite understand why you can't
compare AICs when you change the data. A more familiar example may help.
 First though AIC=-2*log likelihood + 2*number of parameters.  The
log-likelihood value is a function of the data and the model/parameters.
With AIC we want to keep the data constant so we can evaluate differences
due to the model/parameters.  An example, everyone should know is linear
regression.  The log-likelihood for linear regression is a function of the
sum of the squared residuals: (yhat1-y1)^2+(yhat2-y2)^2 + ...+(yhatn-yn)^2
where yhati is the predicted value on the line for the ith observation and
yi is the ith observation. Now consider what happens if I remove or add
another value. Clearly, the sum-of-squared residuals will change (unless
per chance the residual was zero but the likelihood will change because it
includes n). Thus the likelihood value (and thus AIC) will change even if
the model stays the same. Not what you want.

regards --jeff

On Thu, Nov 8, 2012 at 9:07 AM, Chris Merkord <ch...@merkord.com> wrote:

Both but add into that your understanding of the data field collection and
possibility for measurement error.  For example, when I taught a class and
we had them collect data in the field on cactus, I had some come back with
their results and the negative exponential as the best model.  I asked them
whether they thought that the probability of detection was lower on on
either side of their foot than it was right between their legs.  Now the
negative exponential is an easy target but the point is you should use your
knowledge about the data collection. But usually what I'm describing is
fairly obvious from the plot where the adjustments are trying to fit a long
tail and it clearly doesn't fit well near the origin and either way
undershoots or overshoots the first one or two histogram bins. However,
don't over think things too much and get into the paralysis of analysis.
Well-collected data with a small amount of truncation or covariates that
explain the tail are your best bets with the emphasis on good field data
collection and testing. --jeff

messages.body_plain:
Stephen:

The recommended sample size is needed not only for plotting purposes,
but also to provide sufficient information to estimate the detection
function well.  What I mean by estimating well is not only to estimate
parameters of the detection function with high precision but also to
have sufficient degrees of freedom to assess the goodness of the model
fit to data.

In the example you cite with only two or three distance bins, you will
not have sufficient information to measure the fit of your fitted
detection function; e.g., a single parameter half normal model used for
a 3-bin data set will have 3-1-1=1 degree of freedom remaining for
assessing goodness of fit.  Applying a 2 parameter hazard rate model to
the 3-bin data set will produce 3-2-1=0 degrees of freedom for assessing
fit.  See section 3.4.4 of Buckland et al (2001).

So having so few distance bins makes it nearly impossible to assess
model fit regardless of number of detections and so is not a great idea.

Today's list traffic displays the dangers of 'rules of thumb.' Rules are=20
not replacements for common sense.

Lorena--if you can produce a goodness of fit statistic, it is a measure=20
of the fit of your model to data.  Even if it is a single degree of=20
freedom left for fit testing.  That does not make the test 'undesirable'=20
it implies that you have not very much information available to assess fi=
t.

Sandro--you should strive to have a 'large' number of sightings for=20
fitting detection functions.  In your hypothetical (pooled f(0) across=20
strata) you need your target number of sightings for that single=20
detection function.  However you designed your study with geographic=20
(habitat) stratification because you wanted to entertain the possibility=20
that detectability (hence detection functions) differed between=20
habitats.  So you compromised introducing heterogeneity into the=20
detection process by pooling data across habitats in return for boosting=20
sample size for fitting detection functions.  Compromises are a balance=20
of costs and benefits; in the pooling of detection functions, the cost=20
is perhaps small because distance sampling on average produces the=20
correct estimate even when there in heterogeneity in detectability (the=20
pooling robustness property).

General thought about curve fitting (whether a density surface,=20
detection function or any other type of curve fitting exercise).

The data to which you are fitting a curve is a 'sample' as distinct from =

a 'population.'  Hence it is not appropriate to have a highly flexible=20
surface that can morph to any shape; because you are trying to=20
understand the behaviour of the process that gives rise to the data,=20
rather than the data themselves.

Remember your past understanding of regression.  When you have as many=20
coefficients as data points, you fit your points exactly, but the model=20
may predict poorly for situations out of the dataset. Much of what we do =

is intended for prediction purposes, hence over-fitting is something we=20

messages.subject_clean: sampling from roads, shore lines, rivers, vantage points,
messages.body_plain:
Dear List,

Please forgive me for the blatant self promotion of a paper, but I have=20
recently got one accepted that deals with the often overlooked issue of=20
using distance sampling with samplers (lines or points) laid along=20
features with respect to which the animals might respond to. This could=20
lead to potentially severely biased estimates, and it's often the case=20
that we see studies conducted say using roads as transects without=20
properly evaluating the effect of the distribution of the animals with=20
respect to the roads on the density estimates. Often questions on this=20
list hint to the fact that this was the case, but rarely the question is=20
about that particular fact. I argue that quite often that fact should be=20
more worrying than the question being asked.

The paper was written in what I hope to be a style sufficiently=20
appealing for practitioners. The reference is:

Marques, T. A.; Buckland, S. T.; Bispo, R. & Howland, B. Accounting for=20
animal density gradients using independent information in distance=20
sampling surveys Statistical Methods and Applications, 2013. DOI:=20
10.1007/s10260-012-0223-2

Abstract: Distance sampling is extensively used for estimating animal=20
density or abundance. Conventional methods assume that location of line=20
or point transects is random with respect to the animal population, yet=20
transects are often placed along linear features such as roads, rivers=20
or shorelines that do not randomly sample the study region, resulting in=20
biased estimates of abundance. If it is possible to collect additional=20
data that allow an animal density gradient with respect to the transects=20
to be modelled, we show how to extend the conventional distance sampling=20
likelihood to give asymptotically unbiased estimates of density for the=20
covered area. We illustrate the proposed methods using data for a=20
kangaroo population surveyed by line transects laid along tracks, for=20
which the true density is known from an independent source, and the=20
density gradient with respect to the tracks is estimated from a sample=20
of GPS collared animals. For this example, density of animals increases=20
with distance from the tracks, so that detection probability is=20
overestimated and density underestimated if the non-random location of=20
transects is ignored. When we account for the density gradient, there is=20
no evidence of bias in the abundance estimate. We end with a list of=20
practical recommendations to investigators conducting distance sampling=20
surveys where density gradients could be an issue.

(pdf naturally available upon request)

I take the opportunity to ask everyone publishing distance sampling=20
related papers to send me their references (bibtex format preferred!),=20
to be added to the distance sampling reference web page hosted at:

http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distancesamplingreferences/

all the best,

Tiago

messages.body_plain:
The Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling
(CREEM) is hosting two linked workshops in the summer of 2013 in our
purpose-built facilities at the University of St Andrews, Scotland. The aim
of these workshops is to train participants in the latest methods for
design and analysis of distance sampling surveys, including line and point
transects. The workshops are taught by leading researchers in the field,
using industry-standard software.

The first workshop (20-23 August) will run at an introductory level, and
will focus on distance sampling methods, largely described in the standard
reference book "Introduction to Distance Sampling." The workshop will be a
blend of theory and practice and participants will learn how to use the
program "Distance." Participants will gain a solid grounding in both survey
design and methods of analysis for distance sampling surveys.  Note that we
have moved the 'automated survey design' and 'incorporating covariates in
detection function' from the advanced workshop into the introductory
workshop.

The advanced distance sampling workshop (26-29 August) will include
advanced treatment of:  analyses in which detectability on the transect
line is not assumed to be perfect (the so-called g(0) problem) and spatial
(or  density surface) modelling. We will also showcase a series of new R
packages we have developed for performing standard as well as sophisticated
analyses in R. The aim of this workshop is to bring participants up to date
with the latest developments in distance sampling methods and software. It
is also an opportunity for those actively engaged in the design, analysis
and execution of distance sampling surveys to discuss common issues and
problems, and set future research directions. The workshop will be a
combination of lectures and computer sessions, with considerable time for
discussion.

For all workshops, participants are encouraged to bring their own data
sets, and can expect to do some preliminary analyses with their data.
Computer sessions take place in our modern computer classroom (attached to
the seminar room); participants can use our computers or bring their own
laptops.

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

The R library dsm is now available on CRAN as part of it's 2.0 release.
The package implements spatial modelling for distance sampling data as
in Hedley and Buckland ("Spatial Models for Line Transect Sampling",
JABES 2004).

I advise all users of dsm in R (_not_ Distance for Windows) to upgrade.

Version 2.0 fixes a series of bugs, now includes better documentation
and examples. The syntax has been greatly simplified from previous
versions and now operates similarly to the popular mgcv package.

Features include:
  * fitting of models with counts, estimated abundance, density
  * use a detection function fitted with Distance or mrds pacakges
  * standard GAM diagnostics
  * uncertainty estimation using GAM theory or moving block bootstrap
  * easy plotting of both smooths and uncertainty maps
  * use of any smooth basis available to mgcv, including the soap film
smoother for complex regions (peninsulae, islands etc) (and if you're
adventurous you can write you're own)
  * for more information about new features see
http://dill.github.com/posters/dsm-poster-isec2012.pdf
  * for a worked example using marine mammal data, see
https://github.com/dill/dsm/wiki/mexico-analysis

Please do make sure that you have updated to the newest versions of R,
mgcv, Distance and mrds (update.packages() in R) before attempting to
use dsm.

Note that this version of dsm is _not_ compatible with the Windows
program DISTANCE and can only be used in R. It will however be
incorporated into the next major DISTANCE release.

Finally, please do report any bugs to me and I will attempt to fix them
as quickly as possible.

--dave

messages.body_plain:
Oph=C3=A9lie:

Surveys from land of marine organisms present difficulties, one of which=20
you describe.  This is symptomatic of your organisms not being=20
distributed uniformly from your vantage point.  The probability of=20
detecting your organisms is not only a function of your detection=20
probability decreasing at great distances, but the probability of the=20
organisms being located at different distances is also changing.

This challenge is discussed in the following paper:
Marques, T.A., Buckland, S.T., Borchers, D.L., Tosh, D. & McDonald, R.A.=20
(2010) Point Transect Sampling Along Linear Features. /Biometrics/,=20
66:1247-1255

You can view this paper at the Distance bibliography website=20
(http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distancesamplingreferences/)

Standard distance sampling methods (as described by Buckland et al.=20
(2001) are not sufficient for analysing such data.  You need to be able=20
to disentangle detection probability and animal distribution, for which=20
you need additional information.

messages.body_plain:
Christiane:

You note that you are conducting your analysis in R, but it is not clear=20
from your email if you are using the dsm() R package to perform your=20
modelling.  Assuming that you are using dsm(), I further assume that you=20
are using the version of dsm() distributed with Distance 6.0 [which=20
would be dsm version 1.0.5].  That code does employ the moving block=20
bootstrap described in Clark et al. (2003).  And as you note that method=20
of variance estimation is capable of producing extreme predictions.

You might consider use of dsm version 2.0 that is on CRAN as a=20
stand-alone R package.  If you have not included individual-level=20
covariates in your detection function (such as group size), you could=20
consider the use of the function dsm.var.prop() to propagate uncertainty=20
from the detection function step through the spatial modelling step into=20
your final estimates without the use of the bootstrap.  This function=20
uses methods described in Williams et al. (2011) for variance=20
estimation.  Have a look at the package on CRAN, the maintainer of the=20
package, Dave Miller, is working on a paper describing the package, you=20
could contact him off list for more details.

I hope I have answered the question you had in mind.
